title: Bread from the Sky
sum: A month out of Egypt, the people are hungry and wish aloud that they had died by the meat pots of Egypt. God answers the complaint with a gift and a test: "I am about to make bread fall like rain from the sky for you." Quail cover the camp in the evening, and in the morning a fine, flaky layer lies on the ground. "What is it?" they ask, man hu, and the name sticks: manna.

The gift comes with rules. Each person gathers as much as he needs, and no one has too much or too little. Leftovers rot by morning, except on the sixth day, when a double portion keeps through the seventh. Some go out on the Sabbath anyway and find nothing. A jar of manna is set aside for later generations, and the chapter ends by saying Israel ate it for forty years, until they reached the edge of Canaan.
readings: Read as a miracle of providence

God feeds a nation in the desert day by day for forty years, teaching trust: people do not live on bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3). The rules about gathering train the people to depend on God and to rest on his day.
Read as a natural food made holy

Since the 1800s, travelers and scientists have pointed to the sweet honeydew left by insects on tamarisk trees in Sinai, which Bedouin still call mann. On this reading the story remembers a real desert food, enlarged into a sign of God's care.
Read as a lesson in economics

No hoarding, enough for everyone, rest every seventh day: Jewish and Christian readers have long found here a model of a just community. Paul quotes 16:18 when he asks churches to share their wealth (2 Corinthians 8:15).

views.H: A real miracle in the wilderness of Sin, sustaining perhaps two million people for forty years (Joshua 5:12). Natural honeydew could not feed so many, so traditional readers see an act of God beyond nature.
views.M: A small group in the desert could have lived for a season on desert foods such as tamarisk honeydew and migrating quail, which still fall exhausted on the Sinai coast each autumn. The memory grew as the story became all Israel's.
views.C: Source critics divide the chapter between a Priestly layer (the Sabbath rules, the jar "before the testimony," the omer) and an older layer of complaint and test. The jar placed before an ark not yet built (16:34) shows the chapter was written from a later viewpoint. The story teaches the Sabbath before Sinai.
views.J: The rabbis said each person tasted in manna whatever he wished (Yoma 75a), and that it fell near the tents of the righteous and far from the wicked. The two loaves on the Sabbath table recall the double portion, and the cloth over the challah recalls the dew that covered it (16:13–14).
views.X: Jesus calls himself "the true bread from heaven" and "the bread of life" in John 6:31–58, and the Lord's Prayer's "give us today our daily bread" may echo the daily gathering. Paul calls manna "spiritual food" (1 Corinthians 10:3), and Revelation 2:17 promises "hidden manna."

deep.b:
The text says manna appeared with the dew, was fine and flaky like frost, white like coriander seed, tasted like wafers with honey, melted in the sun, rotted overnight, and could be ground, boiled and baked (16:14, 21, 31; Numbers 11:7–9). In 1823 the botanist Christian Ehrenberg described the sweet drops left on tamarisk branches in Sinai by scale insects, and F. S. Bodenheimer (1947) showed that they are secreted honeydew that dries into sticky grains, gathered by Bedouin early in the morning before ants take them. This fits several details (dawn gathering, sweetness, melting) but not others: honeydew appears only for a few weeks in early summer, in small amounts, and does not rot overnight or double on Fridays.

Traditional readers take the differences as the point: the chapter describes a food that behaves like no natural food. Critical readers see a desert memory turned into a teaching about the Sabbath. Both agree the story is less about botany than about trust: "so that he might humble you and test you" (Deuteronomy 8:2–3, 16).

The Sabbath appears here for the first time as a command to Israel, before the Ten Words of chapter 20. The rabbis noticed this and said that Israel had already received some commands at Marah, the Sabbath among them, before Sinai (15:25; Sanhedrin 56b). Christian writers who argued the Sabbath was only for Israel noted that no patriarch is said to keep it; those who argued it was for all people pointed to Genesis 2:2–3, which in this site's Plain English Translation says that on the seventh day God "rested from all the work he had been doing." Critical scholars usually assign the chapter's Sabbath rules to the Priestly writer, who ties creation, manna and the tabernacle to the same weekly rhythm (31:12–17).

echoes: Numbers 11:4–9, 31–34; Deuteronomy 8:2–3, 16; Joshua 5:12; Nehemiah 9:15, 20; Psalm 78:23–29; Psalm 105:40; Matthew 4:4; Matthew 6:11; John 6:31–58; 1 Corinthians 10:3; 2 Corinthians 8:15; Hebrews 9:4; Revelation 2:17

settings.what: The promise of bread and meat
settings.by: The LORD to Moses, then Moses and Aaron
settings.to: Moses; then the whole community of Israelites
settings.when: A month out of Egypt, in the Wilderness of Sin, when they complain of hunger
settings.why: To answer the complaint with a gift and a test. God will rain bread from the sky to see whether Israel will live by his law, and give them meat at evening. Moses and Aaron tell the people that their complaints are against the LORD, not against them.
settings.readers: For Israel, Deuteronomy 8:3 draws the lesson: humans do not live on bread alone.

settings.what: The rules for gathering manna
settings.to: Every Israelite in the wilderness camp, each person gathering for those in his tent
settings.when: The first morning the manna appears
settings.why: To give the rule: an omer for each person, as much as each eats, and none kept until morning. It answers the fear of want. Those who gathered much had nothing left over, and those who gathered little did not run short. Hoarded manna rotted.
settings.readers: For Israel this was a lesson in trusting God for daily bread. Paul uses it to urge sharing (2 Corinthians 8:15).

settings.what: The first Sabbath
settings.to: The chiefs of the community and all the people in the camp
settings.when: The sixth and seventh days of the manna
settings.why: To teach the Sabbath before Sinai. Gather double on the sixth day, bake and boil it, and rest on the seventh, when no manna will fall. It binds everyone in the camp, and the LORD rebukes those who go out anyway. The rule answers how a people fed day by day can stop for a day: God provides for the day of rest.
settings.readers: For Israel the Sabbath was older than the law at Sinai, a gift given in the wilderness.

settings.what: The command to keep a jar of manna
settings.to: The people, then Aaron
settings.when: After the manna has become daily food
settings.why: To keep a full omer of manna before the LORD, so that later generations can see the bread God fed them in the wilderness. Aaron places the jar before the testimony.
settings.readers: For Israel, already in the land and no longer eating manna (16:35), the jar was a witness to God's care in the desert.

title: Water from the Rock, War with Amalek
sum: At Rephidim there is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses so fiercely that he fears they will stone him. God tells him to take the staff that struck the Nile and strike a rock at Horeb, with God himself standing on it. Water pours out. Moses names the place Massah and Meribah, "Testing" and "Quarrel," because they asked, "Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?"

Then Amalek attacks. Joshua leads the fight while Moses stands on a hill with the staff of God. When his hands are raised, Israel wins; when they drop, Amalek wins, so Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset. God tells Moses to write a record that Amalek's memory will be wiped out. Moses builds an altar and calls it "The LORD Is My Flag."
readings: Read as faith under pressure

Both halves ask the same question: is the LORD here with us? In the first, God answers grumbling with water; in the second, Israel wins only while Moses' hands are raised. The Mishnah says the hands did not win the war by themselves: when Israel looked upward and set their hearts on God, they won (Rosh Hashanah 3:8).
Read as Christ the rock and the cross

Paul says the rock that followed Israel "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Early Christian writers saw in Moses' outstretched arms the sign of the cross, and in Joshua, whose name in Greek is Jesus, a picture of the coming savior (Barnabas 12; Justin, Dialogue 90).

views.H: Real events near Sinai: water from a rock at Horeb and Israel's first battle. Amalek was a real desert people, named again in Judges and Samuel until Saul and David fought them.
views.M: Memories of desert hardship and feuds with raiding tribes of the Negev, gathered around place names that sound like "testing" and "quarrel." Numbers 20:1–13 tells a second Meribah story at Kadesh, which suggests a place tradition told in more than one way.
views.C: Two stories joined: a place-name story (Massah and Meribah, also in Deuteronomy 33:8 and Psalm 95:8) and an old war tradition explaining Israel's lasting hostility to Amalek (Deuteronomy 25:17–19; 1 Samuel 15). The written record in 17:14 is the first mention of Moses writing.
views.J: Amalek became the archetype of senseless hatred of Israel; the passage is read on Purim, since Haman is called an Agagite, a descendant of Amalek's king (Esther 3:1). The command to remember Amalek is counted among the 613 commandments. The rabbis also taught that no living people today can be identified as Amalek (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4).
views.X: The rock struck once and giving water becomes a picture of Christ, "struck" and pouring out the Spirit (John 7:37–39; John 19:34). Psalm 95, with its warning about Massah and Meribah, is quoted in Hebrews 3:7–4:11 as a call to faith "today."

deep.h: What do we do with Amalek?
deep.b:
The chapter ends with God's vow to "wipe out, yes, wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky" (17:14) and a war "one generation after another" (17:16). Deuteronomy 25:17–19 turns this into a command, and 1 Samuel 15 tells how Saul was rejected for sparing King Agag. Modern readers rightly find a command to destroy a whole people disturbing.

Jewish tradition has read it in several ways. The Mishnah's principle that the Assyrian king Sennacherib "mixed up the nations" (Yadayim 4:4) was used to say that ancient peoples can no longer be identified, so the command cannot be carried out against any people today. Many teachers turned Amalek into a symbol of evil within and without, the doubt that asks "Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?" (17:7). Others warn that calling any modern enemy "Amalek" has been used to justify violence, and reject that use. Christian readers have mostly spiritualized the passage as the battle against sin, won by prayer, while critical scholars read it as the memory of a long border feud written in the language of holy war common in the ancient Near East, as on the Moabite Mesha stone.

echoes: Numbers 20:1–13; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 8:15; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Deuteronomy 33:8; 1 Samuel 15; Psalm 78:15–20; Psalm 95:8–9; Psalm 105:41; Psalm 114:8; Isaiah 48:21; John 7:37–39; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Hebrews 3:7–4:11

settings.what: The quarrel at Massah and Meribah
settings.by: The people, Moses and the LORD
settings.to: Moses; then the LORD; then Moses with the elders of Israel
settings.when: At Rephidim, where there is no water
settings.why: The people demand water. Moses asks why they test the LORD and cries out that they are about to stone him. God tells him to take the staff and strike the rock at Horeb with the elders watching. The place is named for the people's question, whether the LORD is with them or not.
settings.readers: For Israel the place became a warning, sung in worship (Psalm 95:8–9). Paul says the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

settings.what: The oath against Amalek
settings.to: Moses, who is to write it and read it to Joshua; then Israel
settings.when: After the battle at Rephidim
settings.why: To have it written in a scroll that God will wipe out the memory of Amalek. Moses names the altar The LORD Is My Flag, for the LORD will war with Amalek generation after generation. It is the first time Exodus tells of writing.
settings.readers: For Israel the oath bound its memory, not just one battle, and explained a long enmity (Deuteronomy 25:17–19; 1 Samuel 15).

title: Jethro's Advice
sum: Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, hears what God has done and brings Moses his wife Zipporah and their two sons. Moses tells him the whole story, and Jethro rejoices: "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods." He offers a burnt offering, and Aaron and the elders of Israel eat a meal with him "before God."

The next day Jethro watches Moses judge the people from morning to evening and says, "The way you are doing this is not good." He advises Moses to teach the people God's decrees and to appoint capable, God-fearing, honest men as judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, keeping only the hardest cases for himself. Moses takes the advice, and Jethro goes home.
readings: Read as wisdom from outside

Israel's first system of justice comes from a foreign priest. Jewish and Christian readers have drawn from this that truth can be learned from anyone; the rabbis counted Jethro as a model convert, and some said the Torah portion is named after him for that reason.
Read as a leadership lesson

"You can't carry it by yourself" (18:18). The chapter is often used to teach delegation, and the qualities of the judges (able, God-fearing, trustworthy, hating bribes) reappear in Deuteronomy 1:13–17 and in the qualifications for leaders in Acts 6:3 and 1 Timothy 3.

views.H: A real visit by Moses' father-in-law, either before Sinai, as the order suggests, or after the law was given, since 18:16 speaks of "decrees and teachings" and Deuteronomy 1:9–18 places the appointment of judges later.
views.M: The friendly bond between Israel and Midian, and Jethro's sacrifice to the LORD, support the "Midianite hypothesis": that the worship of the LORD came to Israel partly through Midianite or Kenite priests in the region south of Canaan.
views.C: Many scholars see the story as an old tradition about the origins of Israel's courts, kept despite the later hostility to Midian (Numbers 25; 31). Its placement before Sinai may be thematic, setting human wisdom before divine law.
views.J: The rabbis debated whether Jethro came before or after the giving of the Torah (Zevachim 116a) and what he "heard" (18:1): the splitting of the sea, or the war with Amalek. The Mekhilta lists seven names for him and calls him a righteous convert.
views.X: Church writers saw Jethro as a picture of the nations coming to faith, sharing a meal before God with Israel's elders, as Gentiles would join the church.

deep.h: Where did Israel's worship of the LORD begin?
deep.b:
Moses first meets God while keeping Jethro's flocks at "the mountain of God" in Midian (3:1). Here Jethro praises the LORD, offers sacrifices, and leads a sacred meal with Aaron and the elders (18:12). Since the 1800s, scholars have asked whether Israel learned the name and worship of the LORD from Midianites or Kenites, Jethro's people (Judges 1:16). Egyptian lists from the 1300s BC mention "the land of the Shasu of Yhw" in the region of Edom and Seir, and old poems say the LORD came "from Seir," "from Teman" or "from Sinai" (Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:3).

Supporters of the theory point to these southern links. Critics answer that the Bible never says Israel took its faith from Midian, that Jethro here confesses the LORD as something new ("Now I know," 18:11), and that later texts treat Midian as an enemy. Traditional readers see Jethro as a God-fearer like Melchizedek, a foreign priest who recognizes the true God.

echoes: 2:16–22; 3:1; 4:18–20; Numbers 10:29–32; Deuteronomy 1:9–18; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11; 1 Samuel 15:6; Acts 6:1–6; 1 Timothy 3:1–13

settings.what: Jethro's blessing
settings.to: Moses (and, by 18:12, Aaron and the elders)
settings.when: After Moses tells him the whole story
settings.why: To bless the LORD for rescuing Israel and to confess that the LORD is greater than all the gods. Jethro then offers sacrifice and eats with Aaron and the elders before God.
settings.readers: For Israel, a foreign priest made the confession Pharaoh would not. The nations, too, could come to know the LORD.
views: Jewish tradition makes Jethro a convert to Israel's faith.
Some scholars think the worship of YHWH came to Israel from the Midianites or Kenites, perhaps through such a priest.

settings.what: Jethro's counsel on judges
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: The next day, when Moses sits judging the people from morning to evening
settings.why: To tell Moses he will wear himself out. Jethro advises him to teach the people God's rules and laws. He should appoint men of worth who fear God and hate crooked profit as judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Only the hard cases should come to Moses. It answers a practical problem of a growing people: justice for everyone, not only for those who can reach the leader.
settings.readers: For Israel, its system of judges and elders looked back to this counsel (Deuteronomy 1:9–18). Good order could be learned even from a foreigner.

title: At the Foot of the Mountain
sum: In the third month after leaving Egypt, Israel camps facing the mountain. God's first words there are an offer: "You have seen with your own eyes what I did to Egypt. I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me." If Israel keeps his covenant, they will be his "own private treasure" out of all the peoples, "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." The people answer as one: "Whatever the LORD has said, we will do!"

Then come three days of preparation: washing clothes, staying away from women, and a boundary around the mountain that no one may cross. On the third day there is thunder and lightning, a thick cloud, and a horn blast that grows louder and louder. The mountain smokes like a furnace and quakes. Moses speaks, and God answers him with a voice, and Moses goes down to warn the people once more not to break through.
readings: Read as a wedding

The rabbis compared Sinai to a wedding: God the groom, Israel the bride, the mountain held over them like a wedding canopy, the tablets as the marriage contract. The prophets use the same picture (Jeremiah 2:2; Hosea 2:14–20).
Read as a treaty

Scholars since George Mendenhall (1955) have compared the Sinai covenant with ancient treaties between a great king and a lesser one: a history of the king's kindness (19:4), stipulations (chapters 20–23), blessings and witnesses (chapter 24).
Read as terror and holiness
The boundary, the fire and the trembling teach that God's holiness is dangerous. Hebrews 12:18–21 recalls the scene to contrast it with Mount Zion, while saying God remains "a fire that eats."

views.H: Israel met God at a real mountain in the Sinai Peninsula or in Arabia, and heard his voice. Traditional Christian pilgrimage places it at Jebel Musa in southern Sinai.
views.M: A group of Israel's ancestors experienced something at a holy mountain in the south that shaped their worship, and the memory of it gathered all of Israel's law around it.
views.C: The chapter combines several sources, with Moses going up and down the mountain repeatedly (19:3, 7, 8, 14, 20, 25). The volcanic or storm imagery uses the language of the ancient storm-god, transferred to the LORD. Sinai may be more a theological place than a location on a map.
views.J: Israel arrived "on this same day" (19:1), and the rabbis read that the Torah should be as new to each generation as on the day it was given. Shavuot celebrates the giving of the Torah, traditionally on the sixth of Sivan; all Jewish souls, born and unborn, were said to stand at Sinai (Deuteronomy 29:14–15).
views.X: Luke's account of Pentecost, with its sound from heaven and tongues of fire fifty days after Passover, has often been read as a new Sinai (Acts 2:1–4). 1 Peter 2:9 applies the Greek phrases "royal priesthood" and "holy nation" to the church, and Revelation 1:6 to all believers.

deep.b:
The Bible gives no map. It calls the mountain Sinai or Horeb, places it in the wilderness a journey of some days from Egypt and "eleven days" from Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 1:2), and links it to Midian (3:1). At least a dozen sites have been proposed. The main candidates:

  • Jebel Musa (about 2,285 meters) in southern Sinai, beside St. Catherine's Monastery. It has been the Christian tradition since at least the 300s AD, when pilgrims such as Egeria visited, and it remains the most widely accepted site.
  • Jebel Serbal, also in southern Sinai, favored by some early Christians and some modern scholars.
  • Northern Sinai sites such as Jebel Sin Bishar (proposed by Menashe Har-El) or Jebel Helal, nearer the route to Kadesh.
  • Har Karkom in the Negev, where Emmanuel Anati found many shrines and rock drawings, though mostly from the third millennium BC, far earlier than most dates for the exodus.
  • Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in the region of ancient Midian: Paul says "Mount Sinai in Arabia" (Galatians 4:25), though "Arabia" in his day included the Sinai Peninsula. A volcanic peak would fit the fire and smoke, and Jebel al-Lawz has become popular in some modern circles, though professional archaeologists have not accepted the claims made for it.

Traditional Jewish thought has often found it fitting that the mountain's place was forgotten: the Torah, not a holy site, is what Israel carries.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the mountain that walks
deep.b: My own reading, which builds on what several scholars (Jon Levenson among them) have said: Exodus is built to move the mountain. In chapter 19 God's presence is on Sinai in cloud, fire and thunder, and no one may touch it. In chapters 25 to 40 the same cloud and glory settle into a tent that travels with Israel (40:34–38), and the boundaries of the mountain (the people below, the elders partway, Moses at the top) become the courtyard, the holy place and the holy of holies. If that is right, the loss of Sinai's location is no accident. The book does not want Israel to go back to the mountain; it wants the mountain to go with Israel.

echoes: 3:1–12; Deuteronomy 4:9–40; Deuteronomy 5:2–5; Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4–5; 1 Kings 19:8–18; Psalm 68:7–8; Jeremiah 2:2; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 7:38; Galatians 4:24–26; Hebrews 12:18–29; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6; Revelation 5:10

settings.what: The covenant offer at Sinai and the people's answer
settings.by: The LORD, calling from the mountain; then the people
settings.to: Moses, to tell the house of Jacob, the Israelites camped before the mountain; then Moses
settings.when: In the third month after leaving Egypt
settings.why: To offer a covenant. God reminds them what he did to Egypt, and how he lifted them up on the wings of eagles and brought them to himself. If they listen and keep his covenant, they will be his own private treasure out of all the peoples, "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." The offer comes before the law and grounds it in rescue. The people answer together, "Whatever the LORD has said, we will do!"
settings.readers: For Israel this was its calling: to be holy among the nations. 1 Peter 2:9 gives the same titles to the church.

settings.what: The rules for meeting God
settings.to: Moses; then all the people in the camp, and the priests
settings.when: The three days before God comes down, and when he has come down on the mountaintop
settings.why: To prepare the people. They must wash their clothes and not come near a woman. A boundary is set around the mountain, and anyone who touches it dies. When God has come down, he warns again that neither the people nor the priests may break through to see him; only Moses and Aaron may come up. The rules bind every Israelite in the camp. They answer the danger of holiness: God's presence is life to those who keep its limits and death to those who rush in.
settings.readers: For Israel the same graded holiness shaped the tabernacle and the Temple. Only the priests could enter the holy place, and only the high priest the most holy place.

title: The Ten Words
sum: God speaks to all the people: "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves." Then come the Ten Words, as the Bible itself calls them (34:28): no other gods, no images, no empty use of God's name, the Sabbath, honor for parents, and no murder, adultery, theft, lying testimony or craving what belongs to a neighbor. Most are short commands that begin "You must not."

The people see the thunder, the lightning and the smoking mountain and stand far off, terrified. "Let it be you who speaks with us," they tell Moses. He answers that God has come to test them so that the fear of him will keep them from sinning, and he goes into the deep darkness where God is. The chapter ends with the start of the Covenant Code: no gods of silver or gold, and an altar of earth or uncut stone.
readings: Read as the core of the covenant

The Ten Words open with grace ("I brought you out") before any command. They are spoken by God directly to all the people, written by God's finger (31:18), and kept in the ark. Every later law can be read as commentary on them.
Read as universal moral law

Christian tradition, from Augustine to Aquinas, Luther and Calvin, has treated the Ten Commandments as a summary of the natural moral law written on every heart (Romans 2:14–15), and catechisms in every major church are built around them.
Read in its ancient setting

Critical scholars compare the Ten Words to ancient treaty stipulations and to the short lists of curses in Deuteronomy 27:15–26. Many think they once existed in a shorter form, perhaps ten brief commands, later expanded with reasons.

views.H: God spoke these words audibly from Sinai to the whole nation and later wrote them on two stone tablets. Deuteronomy 5 is Moses' retelling forty years later.
views.M: A short list of basic commands may go back to Israel's early days, but its present wording shows the later concerns of the kings and the exile (the image ban, the Sabbath's link to creation).
views.C: The Decalogue as we have it is usually dated no earlier than the 700s BC, and it shows the influence of Deuteronomy. Its two versions (Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5) show editing at work, and its central place may be a late development.
views.J: Jews count 20:2 ("I am the LORD your God") as the first of the Ten Words. The rabbis taught that Israel heard the first two commands from God's mouth and the rest through Moses (Makkot 24a), and that all 613 commandments are contained in the ten. Jews in the Temple recited them daily with the Shema (Mishnah Tamid 5:1), a practice later stopped so that no one would claim only these were from Sinai (Berakhot 12a).
views.X: Jesus quotes the second table to a rich young man (Mark 10:19) and deepens the commands on murder and adultery (Matthew 5:21–30). Paul sums them up in love (Romans 13:8–10). Christians disagree about the Sabbath: most keep Sunday as the Lord's Day; some keep Saturday.

deep.h: How the Ten Words are counted
deep.b:
The Bible says there are ten (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; Deuteronomy 10:4) but does not number them, and the text has more than ten commands. Four main systems divide them:

Jewish (Talmud, Mekhilta)Catholic and Lutheran (Augustine)*Reformed, Anglican, Orthodox (Philo, Josephus, Origen)Samaritan
1"I am the LORD" (20:2)No other gods and no images (20:3–6)No other gods (20:3)No other gods and no images (20:3–6)
2No other gods and no images (20:3–6)God's name (20:7)No images (20:4–6)God's name
3God's nameSabbathGod's nameSabbath
4SabbathParentsSabbathParents
5ParentsMurderParentsMurder
6MurderAdulteryMurderAdultery
7AdulteryStealingAdulteryStealing
8StealingFalse witnessStealingFalse witness
9False witnessYour neighbor's wife (Lutheran: his house)False witnessCraving
10Craving (20:17)Your neighbor's goods (Lutheran: his wife and all the rest)Craving (20:17)An altar on Mount Gerizim (see the variant at 20:17)

The differences matter. Separating the image ban (Reformed) supported the removal of images from churches; joining it to the first command (Catholic, Lutheran) treats it as part of the ban on other gods. *Catholics and Lutherans agree on 1–8. The Catholic split of the last command follows Deuteronomy 5:21, which puts the wife first and uses a different verb for property; Luther's catechisms keep the order of Exodus 20:17, so their ninth is the house and their tenth the wife, servants, animals and everything else. The Jewish count makes the first "word" a statement of who God is, not a command at all.

deep.h: Two tablets: how were the words divided?
deep.b: The Ten Words were written "on both sides" of two tablets (32:15), and readers have long asked what each held. Philo and the Mekhilta put five on each: duties to God, including honoring parents, who share in creating life, then duties to people. The Mekhilta paired them across the tablets: "I am the LORD" opposite "You must not murder," since murder destroys God's image. Augustine divided them three and seven, matching the love of God and of neighbor in Matthew 22:37–40. Calvin and the Reformed tradition divided them four and six. In 1963 Meredith Kline argued from ancient treaties, which were made in duplicate, one copy for each party, that each tablet held all ten: one copy for God and one for Israel, both kept in the ark. No division is certain.

Deuteronomy 5:6–21 repeats the Ten Words with differences:

  • Sabbath: "Remember" (Exodus) and "Keep" (Deuteronomy). The reason is creation in Exodus (20:11) and the release from slavery in Egypt in Deuteronomy (5:15), and Deuteronomy adds the ox and the donkey and "Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do." The rabbis said God spoke "remember" and "keep" in a single utterance (Shevuot 20b), and the Sabbath hymn Lekha Dodi sings it.
  • Parents: Deuteronomy adds "as the LORD your God commanded you" and "that it may go well with you."
  • False witness: ed shaqer, "lying witness" (Exodus), and ed shav, "empty witness" (Deuteronomy).
  • Craving: Exodus lists the house first, then the wife; Deuteronomy puts the wife first, uses a second verb ("desire") for the house, and adds "his field."
  • Connections: Deuteronomy joins the second table with "and" ("and you must not commit adultery").

Traditional readers see Deuteronomy as Moses' own retelling, with the reasons adapted for a people about to own land and slaves. Critical scholars usually see the Deuteronomic form as older in several places, with Exodus 20:11 a later Priestly addition linking the Sabbath to Genesis 1.

The Talmud says that 613 commandments were given to Moses: 365 negative ones, like the days of the solar year, and 248 positive ones, like the parts of the human body (Makkot 23b). The count is traditional rather than obvious, and medieval scholars listed the commands differently; the best-known list is Maimonides' Book of the Commandments, which counts 20:2 as the command to believe in God. Saadia Gaon and others wrote poems arranging all 613 under the Ten Words, and Philo had already organized his Special Laws under them. In Christian teaching, Aquinas distinguished the moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binding), the ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ) and the judicial law (Israel's civil laws, no longer binding as such). The Catechism of the Catholic Church, Luther's catechisms and the Westminster catechisms all teach the moral life through the ten.

echoes: 31:18; 32:15–19; 34:1, 28; Leviticus 19:1–18; Deuteronomy 4:13; Deuteronomy 5:6–21; Deuteronomy 10:1–5; Jeremiah 7:9; Hosea 4:2; Psalm 81:9–10; Matthew 5:17–37; Matthew 19:16–19; Mark 10:19; Romans 2:21–22; Romans 7:7; Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2–3; James 2:10–11

settings.what: The Ten Words
settings.to: All Israel, the people gathered below Mount Sinai
settings.when: On the third day, in thunder and fire
settings.why: To set out the core of the covenant. First comes who God is: "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves." Then come ten words for a freed people. They forbid other gods, idols and the empty use of God's name. They command the Sabbath and honor for parents. They forbid murder, adultery, theft, lying testimony and craving. "You" is singular: the words bind each Israelite, men and women. The heads of households answer for the children, slaves, animals and foreigners under them (20:10). The words answer the problem of how former slaves will live as a free people under God.
settings.readers: For Israel the words guarded God's honor, the family, life, marriage, property, the courts and even desire. They carry no court penalties and are not tied to one place, so they bound Israel in the camp and in the land. Jews count 20:2 as the first word; Christians number the words in different ways.
views: Traditional readers hold that God spoke these words to all Israel at Sinai.
Many scholars think a short series of commands goes back to early Israel, with reasons added later. Deuteronomy 5 gives a different reason for the Sabbath.
Others date the list to the time of the prophets or the exile.

settings.what: The people's request for a go-between
settings.to: Moses; then the people
settings.when: As they see the thunder and the smoking mountain
settings.why: The people beg Moses to speak to them instead of God, for fear they will die. Moses tells them not to be afraid: God has come to test them, so that fear of him will keep them from sin.
settings.readers: For Israel the request explained why Moses carries the rest of the law to them. Deuteronomy 5:23–31 tells it at length, and makes it the ground of the prophet's office (Deuteronomy 18:16–18).

settings.what: The law of the altar
settings.to: The Israelites as a whole
settings.when: Right after the Ten Words
settings.why: To forbid gods of silver and gold, and to say how to build an altar. It must be of earth, or of uncut stones, with no steps that would expose the body. It binds every Israelite who offers sacrifice, in every place where God makes his name remembered. It answers how a people without temple or priesthood should worship: simply, without images, and without copying the altars of other nations.
settings.readers: For Israel the law had to be fitted with Deuteronomy 12, which allows sacrifice only at the one place God chooses.
views: Many scholars read 20:24 as allowing altars in many places, as in the days of the judges and Samuel, before worship was centralized.
Traditional readers take it to mean the altar of the camp wherever it moved, or altars at places God approved.

traditions.q: Must Christians keep the Sabbath, and is Sunday the Sabbath?
views: Sunday, the day of the resurrection, fulfills the Sabbath and replaces it for Christians (Catechism 2175–2176). Catholics are bound to attend Mass on Sundays and to rest from work that keeps them from worship and joy (Catechism 2180–2185).
Saturday is still honored as the Sabbath, with a lighter fast and its own place in the liturgy, but Sunday, the eighth day of the new creation, is the Lord's Day of the resurrection.

The Sabbath law was for Israel and is fulfilled in Christ; the church keeps Sunday by its own good order, not by divine command (Augsburg Confession, article 28). Luther taught that the commandment now means to hear and learn God's word gladly.

God moved the Sabbath to the first day at the resurrection, and the Christian Sabbath is to be kept holy all day, resting from work and recreation to worship (Westminster Confession 21.7–8). Continental Reformed churches, following the Heidelberg Catechism (Q103), are less strict, so Reformed practice varies.

The seventh-day Sabbath, set at creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and written in this commandment, still binds all people; no text of Scripture moves it to Sunday (Fundamental Beliefs 20). Adventists keep it from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday.
The first day of the week is the Lord's Day, a Christian institution kept in memory of the resurrection (Baptist Faith and Message, article 8). Seventh Day Baptists, a smaller group, keep Saturday.

title: Laws for Slaves and for Violence
sum: The rulings of the Covenant Code begin with slavery. A Hebrew slave serves six years and goes free in the seventh, though he may choose to stay for life and have his ear pierced at the doorpost. A daughter sold as a slave wife keeps rights to food, clothing and marital relations, or she goes free. Then come laws on killing: murder brings death, but an accidental killer may flee to a place God will appoint.

Striking or cursing parents and kidnapping are capital crimes. The chapter rules on injuries from fights, on a slave beaten to death or maimed, on a pregnant woman hurt in a brawl, and states the principle "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." It ends with the goring ox and the open pit: who pays when an animal or a careless owner causes harm.
readings: Read as justice for its time

Compared with other ancient laws, these rulings limit slavery for fellow Hebrews to six years, punish a master who kills his slave, free a slave whose eye or tooth is knocked out, and treat kidnapping as a capital crime. Many readers see a movement toward human dignity within an ancient system.
Read as a wound in the text

The same chapter calls a slave "his money" (21:21) and lets a master keep the wife and children he gave a slave. Abolitionists and their opponents in the 1800s both quoted these laws, and many readers today say honestly that Scripture here reflects its world in ways that must be judged by its own deeper teaching that every person bears God's image.

views.H: Laws given by God through Moses for a nation about to settle in Canaan, setting limits on practices common in the ancient world. Jesus said Moses permitted divorce "in view of your hard-heartedness" (Matthew 19:8), that is, as an allowance for the people as they were.
views.M: The rulings preserve the customary law of Israelite villages in the period of the judges or early kings, perhaps collected by priests or elders and later placed at Sinai.
views.C: The Covenant Code (20:22 to 23:33) is the oldest law collection in the Bible and closely resembles the laws of Hammurabi and other Mesopotamian codes. David Wright (2009) argued that its authors used Hammurabi's text directly in the 700s BC; others think both drew on shared legal tradition.
views.J: The rabbis read these laws through the oral tradition: "eye for eye" means money compensation (Bava Kamma 83b–84a); the six-year slave is a thief sold to repay his theft (Mekhilta); the ear-piercing marks a man who preferred human masters to God, who said Israel are "my slaves" (Rashi; Kiddushin 22b).
views.X: Jesus quotes "eye for eye" and tells his followers not to resist an evildoer and to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42). Paul tells Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 16). Christians have disagreed sharply about what these texts mean for slavery.

deep.b:
Exodus 21 regulates slavery; it does not abolish it. It distinguishes the Hebrew debt-slave, who goes free after six years (21:2), from a slave woman sold as a wife (21:7–11), and elsewhere Leviticus 25:44–46 allows Israelites to hold foreigners as permanent property. A master who beats a slave so that he dies at once is punished, but if the slave lives on for a day or two, "the slave is his money" (21:20–21).

There are also real limits not found in neighboring codes: release in the seventh year, freedom for a slave whose eye or tooth is destroyed (21:26–27), death for kidnapping a person to sell (21:16), and in Deuteronomy, a ban on returning runaway slaves (Deuteronomy 23:15–16), the opposite of Hammurabi's law, which put to death anyone who sheltered one. The whole book of Exodus is the story of God freeing slaves, and the laws repeatedly tell Israel to remember they were slaves in Egypt.

In the American debates of the 1800s, defenders of slavery cited these chapters as proof that the Bible permitted it, while abolitionists cited 21:16 against the slave trade, Genesis 1:27 and the exodus itself. Mark Noll has called the result a theological crisis: both sides read the same Bible. Jewish law later restricted slavery so much that the Talmud said "whoever buys a Hebrew slave buys a master for himself" (Kiddushin 20a). Many readers today hold that the Bible's deeper principles, the image of God in every person and God as the liberator of slaves, judge the practices these laws tolerated.

deep.h: The Covenant Code and the laws of Hammurabi
deep.b:
The stone stele of Hammurabi, king of Babylon (about 1750 BC), found at Susa in 1901 and now in the Louvre, holds about 280 laws. Many of its cases resemble Exodus 21–22 closely:

  • The goring ox (21:28–32; Hammurabi 250–252; also the Laws of Eshnunna 53–55): an ox that gores without warning brings no penalty on its owner; an ox known to gore makes the owner liable; a slave killed by an ox brings a fixed payment.
  • Striking a pregnant woman (21:22–25; Hammurabi 209–214): a fine for the loss of the fetus, heavier penalties if the woman dies.
  • Eye for eye (21:23–25; Hammurabi 196–200): talion for injuries, though in Hammurabi only between free men of the same class.
  • Striking a father (21:15; Hammurabi 195: the son's hand is cut off).
  • Debt slavery (21:2; Hammurabi 117: release after three years).

The differences are just as striking. Exodus has no different penalties for nobles and commoners, does not punish property crime with death (Hammurabi does), sets the death penalty for kidnapping and for murder with no money substitute, and frames every law as the word of Israel's God rather than of a king. Moshe Greenberg (1960) argued that these differences reflect a different scale of values: human life is beyond price, property is not.

echoes: Genesis 9:5–6; Leviticus 24:17–22; Leviticus 25:39–55; Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 15:12–18; Deuteronomy 19:1–21; Deuteronomy 22:28–29; Deuteronomy 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 24:7; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Matthew 5:38–42; Matthew 15:4; 1 Timothy 1:10; Philemon 15–16

settings.what: Laws on Hebrew slaves
settings.by: The LORD, through Moses: "the rulings you will lay before them"
settings.to: The Israelites, above all the heads of households who acquire Hebrew slaves, and the judges who will apply the rulings
settings.when: Given on the mountain after the Ten Words, for life in the land
settings.why: To limit debt slavery among Israelites. A Hebrew man who is sold, usually for debt, works six years and goes free in the seventh owing nothing. He may choose to stay for life by a rite at the doorpost. A daughter sold as a slave wife keeps her rights to food, clothing and marriage, or she goes free. The problem these laws answer is poverty: a ruined family could sell its labor, but not forever.
settings.readers: For Israel, a people just freed from slavery, these laws came first after the Ten Words because it had to limit slavery among its own. The laws do not end slavery, and they treat men and women differently, which later readers have struggled with. Deuteronomy 15:12–18 and Leviticus 25:39–46 revise them.
views: Many scholars compare the Laws of Hammurabi (paragraph 117), which free family members given for debt in the fourth year. They see Israel's law protecting the poor.
Others stress that the laws still allow owning people, and the American debates over slavery fought over these verses.

Traditional readers date the Covenant Code to Moses. Many critical scholars place it in Israel's early villages or under the kings. David Wright argues that it reworks Hammurabi's laws in the Neo-Assyrian period, between about 740 and 640 BC.

settings.what: Laws on killing and injury
settings.to: Every Israelite, and the elders and judges who try cases in local courts
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: To protect life and limit revenge. Murder brings death. One who kills by accident may flee to a place God will appoint, but a schemer is taken even from the altar. Striking or cursing a parent, and kidnapping, are capital crimes. Injury in a fight is paid for in lost time and healing. A master who kills his slave is punished, and one who blinds a slave or knocks out a tooth must set the slave free. The rule of eye for eye and tooth for tooth makes the penalty fit the harm, no more. It answers the problem of endless blood feud.
settings.readers: For Israel, Jewish law from early times applied the rule of eye for eye as payment of money (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1). Jesus speaks of it in Matthew 5:38–39.
views: Some read 21:23–25 as literal punishment. The rabbis and many scholars read it as a principle of fair compensation.
21:22–23 is debated. The harm may be to the woman only, with a miscarriage fined. Or it may be to the woman or the child, with an early birth fined only if no harm follows.

settings.what: Laws on goring oxen and open pits
settings.to: Farmers and owners of oxen and pits, and the judges who settle their cases
settings.when: For village life in the land
settings.why: To set responsibility for harm done by animals and by carelessness. An ox that kills is stoned. If its owner was warned before, he too is guilty, though a ransom may be set for his life. A slave's death costs thirty shekels. The owner of an open pit pays for an animal that falls in, and a fight between oxen is settled by sharing the loss. The problem is everyday liability in a farming village.
settings.readers: For Israel these rulings stood in a shared legal tradition: the goring ox also appears in the Laws of Eshnunna and of Hammurabi. Israel's law stressed that a human life is not just property.

title: Property, the Vulnerable, and Holiness
sum: The laws turn to property: a thief pays back double or more, a burglar killed at night brings no bloodguilt, and the chapter rules on fire spreading to a neighbor's field, goods left in another's keeping, and borrowed animals. A man who seduces an unbetrothed girl must pay the bride-price and marry her if her father agrees.

Then the tone shifts. Sorcery, sex with animals and sacrifice to other gods are condemned. Israel must not wrong a foreigner, "for you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt," nor mistreat a widow or orphan, for God hears their cry. Loans to the poor carry no interest, and a cloak taken as a pledge must be returned at sunset: "for I am gracious." The chapter ends with God's claim on firstborn sons, firstfruits and holiness.
readings: Read as God's preference for the weak

The heart of the chapter is 22:21–27: the foreigner, the widow, the orphan and the poor. God speaks in the first person: "be sure I will hear his cry," "I am gracious." The prophets build on this (Isaiah 1:17; Amos 2:6–8).
Read as ancient law, hard and humane

The same chapter has the death penalty for sorcery, a seduced girl's fate decided by money and her father, and rules for burglars. Readers who take the Bible seriously must ask what is timeless here and what belongs to the ancient world.

views.H: Divine law for Israel's life in the land, mixing civil, moral and religious rules as one whole under God.
views.M: A collection of village law, with older casuistic ("if a man...") rulings joined to direct commands in God's voice that show the influence of prophets and priests.
views.C: Scholars note the change from case law (22:1–17) to absolute commands and motive clauses (22:18–31), which suggests different stages of writing. The concern for the foreigner and the poor matches Deuteronomy and the prophets of the 700s BC.
views.J: The verse on the foreigner (22:21) is counted by the rabbis among the many places where the Torah warns against wronging a ger, which they read as a convert (Bava Metzia 59b). The ban on interest became the basis of Jewish law on loans, and the law of the burglar was used to derive the principle that one may act to save one's own life.
views.X: Jesus' teaching on lending without expecting return (Luke 6:34–35) and James' "pure religion," caring for orphans and widows (James 1:27), build on this chapter. Christian debates on usury from the Middle Ages to Calvin turned on 22:25.

deep.h: "Do not let a sorceress live" and the witch hunts
deep.b:
Exodus 22:18 (Hebrew 22:17) uses a feminine word, mekhashefah. Ancient Israel, like its neighbors, feared harmful magic, and Deuteronomy 18:10–12 bans all forms of divination. The rabbis applied the law to men and women alike (Sanhedrin 67a) and required strict proof; in practice rabbinic courts almost never carried out death sentences.

In early modern Europe the verse, often translated "Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live" (KJV), was quoted in the trials that killed tens of thousands of people, most of them women, between about 1450 and 1750 (historians such as Brian Levack estimate the executions in the tens of thousands). Historians agree that the Bible was one factor among many: new legal procedures, torture, religious conflict and fear all played a part. Many Christians and Jews today see the witch trials as a terrible example of reading an ancient law without its context or the restraint the tradition itself had built around it.

echoes: 23:9; Leviticus 19:9–18, 33–34; Leviticus 25:35–38; Deuteronomy 10:18–19; Deuteronomy 14:28–29; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Deuteronomy 24:10–22; Psalm 15:5; Psalm 68:5; Isaiah 1:17; Ezekiel 18:8; Amos 2:8; Luke 6:34–35; Acts 23:5; James 1:27
links: Witch trials in the early modern period
Witch trials in the early modern period

settings.what: Laws on theft and property
settings.to: Israelite householders, herders and farmers, those who keep or borrow a neighbor's goods, and the judges who hear cases "before God"
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: To protect property and set fair payment. A thief pays back more than he took: five cattle for an ox and four sheep for a sheep that he slaughtered or sold. A burglar killed at night brings no blood guilt, but after sunrise there is guilt. Damage from grazing or fire is made good. Goods left in trust that go missing are settled by an oath or a hearing before God. The problem is keeping peace among neighbors without police: clear rules for loss and blame.
settings.readers: For Israel, a people of villages and herds, these were the cases of daily life. Jacob's complaint to Laban already assumes the rule on animals torn by beasts (22:13; Genesis 31:39).
views: "Before God" (22:8–9) is read as at the sanctuary, as before the judges (so ancient translations), or as before the household gods.

settings.what: Laws on seduction, sorcery and other gods
settings.to: Israelite men, fathers of daughters, and the whole people
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: A man who seduces a girl not promised in marriage must pay the bride-price and marry her, unless her father refuses. Then come three capital laws. No sorceress may live, no one may have sex with an animal, and no one may sacrifice to other gods. The first law protects a daughter and her family in a world where marriage was a contract between families. The others guard Israel's holiness and loyalty to the LORD.
settings.readers: For Israel these laws marked it off from its neighbors' practices. The sorcery law was later used to justify witch trials in Europe, far from its setting.

settings.what: Laws protecting the foreigner, the widow and the poor
settings.by: The LORD, speaking in his own voice
settings.to: Every Israelite, above all those with power to oppress, to lend or to take a pledge
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: To protect those with no one to defend them. Do not mistreat a foreigner, for Israel were foreigners in Egypt. Do not deal harshly with a widow or a fatherless child, for God will hear their cry. Lend to the poor without interest, and give back a cloak taken as a pledge by sundown. These laws name no court penalty: God himself enforces them, and hears the poor because he is gracious.
settings.readers: For Israel, a society that had just escaped oppression, these laws grounded right conduct in memory. Its own past in Egypt was the reason to protect the weak.

settings.what: Laws on respect, first gifts and holiness
settings.to: Every Israelite
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: Do not treat God with contempt or curse a leader of the people. Give from the harvest and the presses without delay. Give God the firstborn sons, and the firstborn animals on their eighth day. Be a holy people, and do not eat meat torn by wild beasts. The laws tie farm life to God's ownership: the first and best belong to him.
settings.readers: For Israel holiness reached even into what it ate. The rule on torn meat set it apart from its neighbors at every meal.
views: Jewish tradition (the Targums, Rashi) and some translations read the Hebrew word for God here as "judges," in parallel with "a leader." The Septuagint reads "gods."

title: Justice, Rest and the Three Feasts
sum: Justice must be fair in court: no false reports, no following the crowd to do wrong, no favoring the poor or perverting the case of the poor, no bribes. Even an enemy's lost ox or donkey must be returned and helped. Do not oppress the foreigner, "You know the life of a foreigner from the inside." The land rests in the seventh year and the people and animals on the seventh day.

Three times a year all males must appear before the LORD: the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Harvest and the Feast of Ingathering. Do not boil a young goat in its mother's milk. Then God promises a messenger who will guard Israel on the way, bearing God's name, and will lead them into the land. God will send terror and the hornet ahead of them and drive out the peoples little by little. They must make no covenant with those peoples or their gods.
readings: Read as a charter of fairness

The chapter rules out both bias toward the rich and sentimental bias toward the poor (23:3, 6). Justice serves truth, not the crowd. Helping an enemy's animal (23:4–5) is a seed of Jesus' "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44).
Read as the calendar of a farming people

The three pilgrim feasts follow the harvest: barley in spring, wheat in early summer, fruit and grapes in autumn. Later tradition linked them to history: the exodus, the giving of the Torah and the wilderness journey.

views.H: Instructions given at Sinai for life in the land, including the feasts Israel would keep at the sanctuary, and a promise of God's angel to guide them.
views.M: Old agricultural festivals of Canaanite farmers were adopted by Israel and given new meaning as remembrance of the LORD's acts.
views.C: 23:14–19 is one of several festival calendars (34:18–26; Leviticus 23; Deuteronomy 16) that scholars compare to trace the development of Israel's worship from local shrines to one central temple.
views.J: The ban on boiling a kid in its mother's milk (23:19; 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21) is the root of the Jewish laws separating meat and dairy (Chullin 115b). The "angel" in whom God's name dwells was identified by some rabbis with Metatron (Sanhedrin 38b). The three feasts are Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot.
views.X: Christian writers often identified the angel who bears God's name (23:20–21) with the pre-incarnate Christ. Mark 1:2 quotes words from 23:20 joined with Malachi 3:1 for John the Baptist. Malachi 3:1 reads: "Look, I am about to send my messenger, and he will clear a road before me."

deep.h: The young goat and its mother's milk
deep.b: "Do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk" appears three times (23:19; 34:26; Deuteronomy 14:21). No one knows its original reason. Maimonides suggested it opposed a pagan rite (Guide 3.48), and in the 1930s scholars thought a Ugaritic text described one, but later readings of that broken text have made this doubtful. Others see a moral lesson: do not use what nurtures life to cook death, a principle like not taking a mother bird with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6–7). Philo read it as a law of compassion (On the Virtues 142–144). The rabbis read the triple repetition as three bans, on cooking, eating and benefiting from meat with milk (Chullin 115b), and extended it to all meat and dairy, the basis of kosher kitchens today.

echoes: Leviticus 19:15, 33–34; Leviticus 23; Leviticus 25:1–7; Deuteronomy 1:17; Deuteronomy 14:21; Deuteronomy 16:1–20; Deuteronomy 22:1–4; Joshua 24:12; Psalm 82:2–4; Proverbs 25:21; Malachi 3:1; Matthew 5:44; Mark 1:2; Romans 12:20

settings.what: Laws on justice in court and kindness to enemies
settings.to: Witnesses, judges and every Israelite who takes part in the local courts
settings.when: For life in the land
settings.why: To keep the courts honest. There must be no false rumors, no following the crowd, and no tipping the scales for the poor or pushing aside the right of the needy. There must be no bribes and no killing the innocent. In the middle stand two laws about an enemy's ox or donkey: bring it back, and help free it from its load. The problem is that justice fails when people side with a crowd, a friend or whoever pays.
settings.readers: For Israel the laws reached even to personal enemies. They end, as 22:21 began, with the foreigner, whose life Israel knew from its own years in Egypt (23:9).

settings.what: Laws on the Sabbath year, the Sabbath and the three feasts
settings.to: Israelite farmers and households in the land; every male for the pilgrim feasts
settings.when: For the farming year in the land
settings.why: To set Israel's holy times. The land rests in the seventh year so that the poor and the wild animals can eat. People and animals rest on the seventh day, including the slave woman's son and the foreigner. Three times a year every male appears before the LORD, at the Feasts of Unleavened Bread, Harvest and Ingathering. The first fruits go to the LORD's house, and a young goat is not boiled in its mother's milk. The problem is how a farming people keeps time with God and makes rest a gift to the weak.
settings.readers: For Israel these laws set the rhythm of the year. The milk law became the root of the Jewish rules that keep meat and dairy apart (Mishnah Chullin 8).
views: Older scholars thought the milk law opposed a Canaanite ritual known from a text at Ugarit. Ratner and Zuckerman showed that the reading of that text is doubtful.
A boundary between life and death
Others see a law like the one against taking a mother bird with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6–7), which keeps the source of life apart from its death.

settings.what: The promise of the angel and the land
settings.to: Israel, about to leave Sinai for Canaan
settings.when: At the end of the Covenant Code
settings.why: To promise an angel who bears God's name to guard them on the way and bring them in, and to warn them to listen to him. God will drive out the peoples of the land little by little. Israel must make no covenant with them or their gods and must smash their standing stones. The words close the law with promise and warning, as ancient treaties ended with blessings and curses. They answer how a small people will live in a land full of other gods.
settings.readers: For Israel, which did live among the Canaanites and their gods, the warning was its own story (Judges 2:1–3).

title: The Covenant Sealed
sum: Moses tells the people all the LORD's words, and they answer with a single voice: "Every word the LORD has spoken, we will do." He writes them down, builds an altar with twelve standing stones for the tribes, and has young men offer sacrifices. He splashes half the blood on the altar, reads the scroll of the covenant aloud, and when the people say "we will do, and we will listen," he throws the rest of the blood on them: "Here is the blood of the covenant."

Then Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders go up and see the God of Israel, with something like blue lapis under his feet. God does not strike them; they eat and drink in his presence. Moses goes higher to receive the stone tablets, leaving Aaron and Hur in charge. The glory of the LORD settles on the mountain like a fire that eats everything, and Moses enters the cloud for forty days and forty nights.
readings: Read as a covenant ceremony
Reading, agreement, writing, witnesses, sacrifice, a meal: the chapter is a complete ritual of binding. The blood marks both parties, God (the altar) and the people, as joined in one life.
Read as a meal with God

For one moment, Israel's leaders eat in God's presence and live. Jewish tradition sees a glimpse of the world to come (Berakhot 17a); Christians see the Lord's Supper and the wedding banquet of the Lamb.
Read through the cross
Jesus' words over the cup, "my blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:24), deliberately echo 24:8. Hebrews 9:15–22 reads the Sinai blood rite as a pattern fulfilled in Christ's death.

views.H: The covenant between God and Israel was formally sealed at Sinai, and the leaders saw a real vision of God's glory before Moses went up for forty days.
views.M: The ceremony may preserve memories of an early covenant ritual among the tribes, perhaps at a shrine like Shechem (Joshua 24), later attached to Sinai.
views.C: The chapter joins at least two traditions: a covenant meal on the mountain with the elders (24:1–2, 9–11), one of the Bible's oldest and boldest visions of God, and a blood rite at the foot of the mountain (24:3–8). The Priestly writer adds the cloud and glory (24:15–18) that lead into the tabernacle chapters.
views.J: "We will do, and we will listen" (na'aseh venishma) became a byword for Israel's love of the Torah (Shabbat 88a). The chapter is read in synagogues as part of the portion Mishpatim, and Shavuot celebrates the covenant made here. The verse "I will give you the stone tablets, with the law and the command" is used to teach that the Oral Torah was given at Sinai (Berakhot 5a).
views.X: The blood of the covenant points to the Last Supper and the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20). Hebrews 12:18–24 contrasts the terror of Sinai with Mount Zion, where believers come to "Jesus, the go-between of a new covenant, and the blood of sprinkling."

deep.b:
Hebrews 12:18–29 sets two mountains side by side. "You have not come" to a mountain that can be touched, burning with fire, with darkness, gloom, storm, a trumpet and a voice that made the hearers beg not to hear more (Exodus 19:12–19; 20:18–21; Deuteronomy 4:11–12). "You have come" to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, to countless angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, to God the judge, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus and his blood, which "speaks something better than Abel." The writer does not say the God of Sinai has changed: "our God is a fire that eats" (Hebrews 12:29, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24). The difference is access.

Jewish readers have their own pairing of Sinai and Zion. Jon Levenson (1985) showed how the Hebrew Bible itself carries the meaning of Sinai over to Zion, the temple mount, so that covenant and presence meet in Jerusalem (Psalm 68:17; Isaiah 2:3: "from Zion comes teaching"). For the rabbis, Sinai is not surpassed; it is relived every time the Torah is studied.

deep.h: Law and gospel: how Christians read Sinai
deep.b:
Christians agree that the law of Sinai is holy (Romans 7:12) and that Christ fulfills it (Matthew 5:17), but disagree on what that means.

  • Lutheran: Luther distinguished law, which shows sin and drives a person to Christ, from gospel, the promise of forgiveness. The law has a civil use (restraining evil) and a theological use (showing sin), and in later Lutheran teaching a third use, as a guide. Galatians 3:24 calls the law a guardian "until Christ came."
  • Reformed: Calvin taught three uses of the law too, but held the third, guiding believers in gratitude, to be the chief one (Institutes 2.7.12). The moral law of the Ten Commandments remains binding; the ceremonial and civil laws of Israel do not.
  • Catholic and Orthodox: The "old law" was a preparation for the gospel; the "new law" is the grace of the Holy Spirit written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33; Aquinas; Catechism 1965–1974). The Ten Commandments remain the core of the moral life.
  • Others: Some Anabaptist and dispensational traditions see the Mosaic covenant as given to Israel only, with believers under "the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). Many recent scholars of Paul (the "New Perspective") argue that Paul's critique was aimed at the law as a boundary between Jews and Gentiles, not at obedience as such.

In Matthew 5:17–48 Jesus says he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, and then deepens six commands: anger as well as murder, lust as well as adultery, and love for enemies. Romans 7 describes the law as good but powerless against sin, and Galatians 3:17 notes that the promise to Abraham came 430 years before Sinai, so the law cannot cancel it. Jewish readers, for their part, have long rejected the idea that the Torah was a burden: "your law is all my delight" (Psalm 119:77).

deep.h: Shavuot: the feast of the covenant
deep.b: Exodus 19:1 places the arrival at Sinai in the third month, and the rabbis counted from Passover to reach the sixth of Sivan, the day of the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), as the day the Torah was given (Shabbat 86b). The Bible itself links Shavuot only to the wheat harvest (23:16; Leviticus 23:15–21), but the link to Sinai is already present in the Book of Jubilees (Jubilees 6:17–21, second century BC), which makes the feast a yearly renewal of the covenant. Today Jews read Exodus 19–20 in synagogue on Shavuot, read the book of Ruth, and many stay up all night studying Torah (Tikkun Leil Shavuot), a custom spread by the Kabbalists of Safed in the 1500s. Christians celebrate the same feast as Pentecost, the Greek name for "fiftieth," when Acts 2 tells of the Spirit given with wind and fire.

settings.what: The covenant sealed in blood
settings.by: The LORD, then Moses, with the people's answers
settings.to: Moses, about himself, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders; then all the people at the foot of the mountain
settings.when: After Moses has received the Ten Words and the rulings
settings.why: Moses tells the people all the LORD's words and rulings and writes them down. He builds an altar with twelve standing stones and reads the scroll of the covenant. He splashes the blood on altar and people: "Here is the blood of the covenant." Twice the people answer that they will do all the LORD has said. The rite binds all twelve tribes into the covenant as one people.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the day it became the LORD's people by oath. Jesus' words over the cup at the Last Supper echo it (Mark 14:24).
